---
title: "Stage 1 — the study as data"
---

The protocol's content — objectives, endpoints, estimands, arms, populations — expressed as
JSON against a defined model, so that it can be queried, linked to and generated from rather
than only read.

## What this is

The minimum a study definition needs, for the endpoints in scope, is objectives, endpoints,
estimands, arms, population, and the biomedical concepts the endpoints are measured by. That is
a *fragment*, and it is what this study's definition was for its first week. It has since been
generated from the whole restructured protocol, and carries epochs, encounters and a schedule of
activities as well — which is what the schedule tab below is showing. The fragment is the
starting point, and enough for everything from stage 2 onward; the whole is what a protocol
authored to M11 gives you without asking.

Loaded into the builder, the study looks like this:

![The study as the builder reads it. Note the rationale: this fragment was *generated* from the
M11-restructured protocol, and says by what and from which sections.](media/study-overview@739344c.jpg)

The fragment itself declares where it came from:

{{json:study/usdm/toriva-lung-301.usdm.json#study.versions[0].studyDesigns[0].arms[0]}}

That is one arm, exactly as stored. Every other element — objective, endpoint, estimand — has
the same character: a named thing with an identifier that something downstream can point at.

## What you do

**The work:** produce the study definition, then make something read it back. A fragment nothing
consumes has not been tested.

1. Generate the fragment from the structured protocol, or hand-author it for a first pass.
2. Make it available to whatever will consume it.
3. Open it there, and read every part of it back.

*In the application used here:* put the fragment where it looks for studies and add it to the
study manifest; the study then appears as a card, and **Study Overview** renders it tab by tab —
Summary, Arms, Objectives & Endpoints, Schedule of Activities, and two more for the narrative
and the configuration.

## What you should see

A study card, and behind it the objectives and endpoints you put in, each with its text from the
protocol. If a tab is empty, that part of the fragment is missing or is not shaped the way the
reader expects.

### Step into the factory

The definition is `study/usdm/toriva-lung-301.usdm.json`, and beside it `study/usdm/README.md`
records what was learned about the shape USDM v4 has to take for this application to read it —
established from the application's own parser and confirmed by loading, with a tree of where
each thing has to sit.

## What to look out for

**Rendering is the real test, not schema validation.** An application reads particular paths,
and a fragment can satisfy the schema with its content somewhere else that is equally valid.
Here the shape was established by reading the application's parser before writing a line: the
biomedical concepts, for instance, have to sit on the study *version*, not on the design, because
that is where this application looks for them. Load it and look before believing it.

**Hand-author once, then generate.** Writing a fragment by hand teaches the shape faster than
reading the model does, and it is worth doing once for that reason alone. But a hand-authored
fragment is a transcription of prose, and it inherits every ambiguity in the prose silently.
Generating it from a structured protocol makes the transcription step reviewable. What that
bought here is at the end of [stage 0b](stage-0b-restructure-and-regenerate.qmd).
